title: Coupling of Cation and Anion Dynamics in Solid Electrolytes Revealed by Virtual Isotopic Substitution Molecular Dynamics
authors: Xintian Wang, Andrew L. Goodwin, Theodosios Famprikis
abstract: We characterise the interplay between cation-translational and anion-rotational dynamics on the model system $\rm α\text{-}Li_{2}SO_{4}$ through virtual isotopic substitution molecular dynamics (VISMD) simulations. We independently control in turn the lithium translational- and sufate rotational- diffusivity by varying the masses of lithium and oxygen, respectively, showing that both diffusivities exhibit power-law relationships with the masses of each individual component. Changing either diffusivity produces an effect on the other; i.e. there exists a bidirectional coupling between anion and cation diffusive dynamics. From our variable-temperature/variable-mass dataset we demonstrate that the apparent activation energy for lithium diffusion depends strongly on the isotope mass, decreasing with accelerated sulfate dynamics; an observation which provides clear evidence of mode-coupling between cation and anion dynamics.
summary: This work uses molecular dynamics simulations on Li2SO4 to characterize the coupling between lithium ion translation and sulfate anion rotation. By varying component masses using VISMD, the authors demonstrate a clear bidirectional coupling mechanism between these two distinct diffusive modes. This finding provides deep insight into how structural dynamics govern ionic conductivity in solid electrolytes.
main_problem: The study investigates the coupling mechanism between cation translational dynamics and anion rotational dynamics within solid electrolytes.
main_result: The simulations reveal a bidirectional, mode-coupling relationship between the two types of diffusion, suggesting that changes in one dynamic process influence the other.
method: Virtual Isotopic Substitution Molecular Dynamics (VISMD) is employed to independently vary component masses and thus control individual diffusivity rates while preserving the underlying potential energy landscape.
model_or_system: The model system is alpha-Li2SO4, an archetypal rotor-phase solid electrolyte. The analysis focuses on the interplay between Li+ cation translation and SO4 2- anion rotation.
key_observables: Lithium translational diffusivity (D_Li^tr), sulfate rotational diffusivity (D_SO4^rot), power-law scaling exponents, and apparent activation energy for diffusion.
important_parameters: Temperature range (800 K to 1400 K), mass variation factors (varying Li and O masses), and the coupling strength parameter derived from comparing Arrhenius vs. power-law fits.
main_assumptions: The VISMD approach assumes that varying atomic masses while keeping potential parameters constant allows for a meaningful, controlled investigation of dynamic mode interplay.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the structure, the power-law scaling of both diffusivities with component mass, and how the apparent activation energy depends on isotopic substitution, confirming coupling effects.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical problem (coupling in solid electrolytes), details the VISMD methodology for controlling individual diffusion modes, presents results showing bidirectional coupling via mass dependence analysis, and concludes by analyzing the implications of this coupling on activation energies.
why_interesting: While focused on ionic solids, the rigorous mathematical framework developed to relate temperature-dependent Arrhenius behavior to power-law scaling exponents (Chunk 4) provides general tools for analyzing coupled dynamics in complex many-body systems, which has parallels in understanding quantum phase transitions or correlated disorder effects.

Figure 1 exemplifies the structure and dynamics of α-Li2SO4 as probed using molecular dynamics simu- lations at 1000 K. α-Li2SO4 adopts an antifluorite-like crystal structure with sulfate anions arranged in a face- centered-cubic arrangement and lithium cations occupy- ing preferentially the corresponding tetrahedral intersti- tials, consistent with previous experimental and compu- tational results [14, 28–31]. Figure 3 shows the radial distribution functions cal- culated from our VISMD simulations with the extreme (highest and lowest) masses of lithium and oxygen; it is evident that the isotopic substitution has no effect on the average structure of the system as the correspond- ing distribution functions are indistinguishable. Hence, this approach allows us to independently vary the mag- nitude of the translational or rotational diffusion coeffi- cients, while controlling for the chemical interactions and average structure of α-Li2SO4.
